story.title: South Korea Crypto Bill Nears Completion With Exchange and Stablecoin Rules - Bitcoin Foundation

facts.text: On July 15, 2026 — the same day Japan's parliament formally voted to reclassify cryptocurrencies as financial products — South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance announced the National Asset Basic Act, declaring it would rewrite the legal foundation of how the government manages public wealth, and for the first time in 76 years, digital assets would be part of that foundation.
South Korean state assets have grown from 188.3 trillion won in 2001 to more than 1,400 trillion won today, roughly $938 billion in state holdings.
About 16 million South Korean adults in digital asset markets — roughly one-third of the adult population — are active participants, according to a CoinGecko market analysis.
Altcoins represent 85% of domestic crypto activity, while Bitcoin accounts for just 9% and Ethereum for 6% — almost the inverse of most Western markets, according to Kaiko.
Under Japan's former framework, crypto was regulated primarily under the Payment Services Act — treated as a method of payment, not an investment.
Officials described the reform as a shift from preservation to value creation: state assets should be actively managed, not merely stored.

The Financial Services Commission pushed back, warning that such a rule would effectively lock technology firms out of stablecoin issuance and suppress competition — and cited the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, where the majority of licensed stablecoin issuers are electronic money institutions rather than banks, as a counterexample.

The Bank of Korea demanded 51% bank ownership for stablecoin issuers, insisting that financial institutions with existing solvency and anti-money-laundering requirements were the only entities capable of ensuring stability.

The stablecoin usage as deployable liquidity rose sharply in the same window, with the stablecoin market cap to KRW exchange volume ratio rising from 2.8x to 3.6x — a signal that stablecoins are increasingly being used as deployable liquidity rather than speculative instruments.
The South Korea crypto bill nears completion with exchange licensing and stablecoin issuance rules, while its separate crypto tax debate intensifies.
Taxation sits on a separate track in South Korea’s crypto policy debate, and it is getting louder as the digital asset bill advances.
The framework would set licensing regimes for crypto exchanges and rules for issuing stablecoins, so trading platforms and stablecoin issuers fall under one broader legislative effort.
The bill is still a proposal nearing completion, which means the licensing requirements and the stablecoin conditions will be settled as it moves forward.

sources.title: South Korea Folds Crypto Into National Asset Law as Japan Passes Its Own Reform
passages: On July 15, 2026 — the same day Japan's parliament formally voted to reclassify cryptocurrencies as financial products — South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance announced the National Asset Basic Act, declaring it would rewrite the legal foundation of how the government manages public wealth, and for the first time in 76 years, digital assets would be part of that foundation.

The announcement makes South Korea the first sovereign asset management statute to embed cryptocurrency inside a sovereign state asset management law — not as a speculative instrument to be taxed and tolerated, but as a category of property the government is legally obligated to manage alongside land, buildings, and intellectual property.

Market Law: A Structural Gap Readers Need to Understand The NABA is only one half of South Korea's digital asset legislative agenda, and understanding the difference between the two halves matters for anyone operating in or watching Korean markets.
South Korean state assets have grown from 188.3 trillion won in 2001 to more than 1,400 trillion won today, roughly $938 billion in state holdings.
About 16 million South Korean adults in digital asset markets — roughly one-third of the adult population — are active participants, according to a CoinGecko market analysis.

The companion Digital Asset Basic Act — known as the DABA — is the piece that would actually govern how private companies and citizens operate in the crypto market: issuance, trading, custody, supervision, stablecoin licensing, and reserve requirements.
Altcoins represent 85% of domestic crypto activity, while Bitcoin accounts for just 9% and Ethereum for 6% — almost the inverse of most Western markets, according to Kaiko.
Under Japan's former framework, crypto was regulated primarily under the Payment Services Act — treated as a method of payment, not an investment.
Officials described the reform as a shift from preservation to value creation: state assets should be actively managed, not merely stored.

The Financial Services Commission pushed back, warning that such a rule would effectively lock technology firms out of stablecoin issuance and suppress competition — and cited the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, where the majority of licensed stablecoin issuers are electronic money institutions rather than banks, as a counterexample.

The Bank of Korea demanded 51% bank ownership for stablecoin issuers, insisting that financial institutions with existing solvency and anti-money-laundering requirements were the only entities capable of ensuring stability.

The stablecoin usage as deployable liquidity rose sharply in the same window, with the stablecoin market cap to KRW exchange volume ratio rising from 2.8x to 3.6x — a signal that stablecoins are increasingly being used as deployable liquidity rather than speculative instruments.
